text: Yes, at least until the age of fifteen or sixteen. Without some history, it's hard to understand why countries have the borders, languages and conflicts they have today. The problem is that it's often taught as a list of dates to memorise. If lessons focused more on causes and ordinary people's lives, far fewer students would find it boring.

text: I think they are, because seeing a real object is very different from seeing a photo online. You notice the size, the texture and the age of things. But many museums need to change. Interactive exhibits, evening events and good audio guides in several languages would attract young people who currently see museums as dusty places for school trips.

text: We can, but we often choose not to. History shows clearly, for example, that economic crises and extreme inequality tend to lead to social unrest, yet similar mistakes keep happening. I think the problem is that each generation believes its situation is completely new. Studying history won't prevent every mistake, but it at least helps people recognise warning signs earlier.

text: Often they do, because they're made to entertain, not to educate. Writers add romance, simplify complicated events and make the heroes more attractive than they really were. Still, I think they're useful if they make people curious enough to read about what actually happened. The danger is only when viewers take everything on screen as fact.

text: Ideally, yes, at least for children, students and pensioners, because heritage belongs to everyone and shouldn't depend on income. Some countries have free national museums, and visitor numbers there are very high. But maintaining old buildings is expensive, so a small fee for foreign tourists, combined with government funding, seems like a fair compromise.
